subject: chemistry
title: Magnesium and acid: the squeaky pop

idea.text: Magnesium is more reactive than hydrogen, so it pushes hydrogen out of hydrochloric acid. The hydrogen bubbles off as a gas, and you can prove it is hydrogen because it burns with a squeaky pop.
idea.analogy: Like musical chairs: magnesium takes hydrogen's seat in the acid, and hydrogen is left standing, so it bubbles away as a gas.

steps.title: Put on goggles
steps.instruction: 1 M hydrochloric acid is corrosive. Goggles on.

steps.title: 5 mL acid into the tube
steps.instruction: Pour about 5 mL of acid into the reaction tube, gently.

whatIf.order: Without goggles, one splash in the eye can cause serious, sometimes permanent, damage within seconds. That's why goggles go on before you open any bottle.
whatIf.rate: A fast pour into a narrow test tube splashes acid up the sides and out of the top.
whatIf.overshoot: More acid fills the tube higher, so the fizzing can froth over the top. 5 mL is plenty.
whatIf.quantity: The amount of acid changes how long the fizzing lasts. With too little, some magnesium may be left unreacted.

explore.if: use 2 M acid instead of 1 M
explore.then: The fizzing is faster and the tube gets hotter, because acid particles hit the magnesium more often. More gas, sooner.
Very slow fizzing: there are ten times fewer acid particles, so you might not collect enough hydrogen for a pop.

steps.title: Drop in the magnesium
steps.instruction: Add a 2 cm piece of magnesium ribbon (about 0.05 g).

whatIf.order: Add the acid first so the magnesium has something to react with.
whatIf.overshoot: More magnesium makes more hydrogen and more heat, and the tube can froth over. A 2 cm strip is plenty.
whatIf.quantity: More magnesium makes more gas and heat; less makes less. A 2 cm strip is about right for one test tube.

explore.if: use magnesium powder instead of ribbon
explore.then: Powder has a much bigger surface area, so the reaction is much faster and hotter. It can fizz violently.
Nothing happens. Copper is less reactive than hydrogen, so it can't push hydrogen out of the acid.

steps.title: Collect the gas
steps.instruction: Straight away, hold the collection tube upside down over the reaction tube. Hydrogen is lighter than air and rises into it.

whatIf.order: Add the magnesium first. Until then there's no gas to collect.

explore.if: hold the collection tube the right way up
explore.then: Hydrogen is much lighter than air, so it floats up and out of the tube. It must be upside down to trap the gas.
Most of the hydrogen escapes into the room first, so you might not collect enough for a pop.

steps.title: Light the Bunsen
steps.instruction: Light the Bunsen burner so you can light a splint.

explore.if: use a match instead of the burner
explore.then: That works too. The burner is just a steady flame for lighting the splint.

steps.title: Light a splint
steps.instruction: Hold the splint in the flame until it catches.

whatIf.order: Light the burner first: the splint needs a flame to catch.

steps.title: The pop test
steps.instruction: Bring the lit splint to the mouth of the collection tube.

whatIf.order: You need both ready: hydrogen collected in the tube and a burning splint. Otherwise there's nothing to pop.

explore.if: use a glowing splint instead of a burning one
explore.then: A glowing splint relights in oxygen, not hydrogen. Hydrogen needs a lit flame to make its pop.

explore.if: collect pure hydrogen with no air in the tube
explore.then: The loudest pop comes from hydrogen mixed with some air. A tube of almost pure hydrogen may just burn quietly at the mouth.

observations.whatHappened: The magnesium fizzed and shrank as bubbles streamed off it, and the tube felt warm. The collected gas burned with a squeaky pop.
observations.why: Magnesium is more reactive than hydrogen, so it pushes hydrogen out of the acid. The metal becomes Mg²⁺ ions in solution and hydrogen gas bubbles off. The reaction gives out heat. Hydrogen mixed with air burns very fast, which makes the pop.

prompts.question: Which gas gives a squeaky pop with a lit splint?
prompts.explain: Hydrogen burns with a pop. Oxygen relights a glowing splint; CO₂ puts it out.

prompts.question: The tube warmed up. The reaction is...
prompts.explain: It releases energy as heat, so it is exothermic.

captions.text: Goggles on, then 5 mL of 1 M hydrochloric acid.
captions.why: Only a small volume is needed: the reaction makes plenty of gas.
captions.safety: 1 M hydrochloric acid is corrosive and can damage eyes, so goggles go on first.

captions.text: Drop in the magnesium and trap the gas straight away.
captions.why: Magnesium + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + hydrogen. The fizzing is hydrogen gas bubbling out.
captions.safety: Hydrogen is lighter than air, so the collection tube is held upside down over the reaction tube to catch it as it rises.

captions.text: Light a splint while the gas collects...
captions.why: The splint has to be burning when it meets the hydrogen. Feel the tube: it's warm, because the reaction is exothermic.
Hydrogen mixed with air burns so fast it makes a tiny explosion: the pop. The only product is water.
